:::{#def-random-effect}
#### Random effect

A **random effect** is a model term
that treats the groups in the data
as a sample from a larger population of groups:
each group's effect is a random variable,
and the groups' effects are drawn from a common distribution,
such as
$$
\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_a \siid \ndist{0, \sigma_\alpha^2}.
$$
The parameters of interest are then the parameters of that distribution,
especially its variance $\sigma_\alpha^2$,
rather than the effects of the particular groups in the data
[@rocke2021epi204].
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-random-effect}
#### Patient random effects

Suppose each of 20 patients has their systolic blood pressure measured several times,
and patient $i$'s mean blood pressure is $\mu + \alpha_i$,
with $\mu = 120$ mmHg and patient random effects
$\alpha_i \siid \ndist{0, \sigma_\alpha^2}$, with $\sigma_\alpha = 10$ mmHg.
About 95% of a normal distribution lies within 1.96 standard deviations of its mean,
so about 95% of patients in the population have mean blood pressures between:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu \pm 1.96\,\sigma_\alpha
&= 120 \pm 1.96 \cdot 10
&& \text{(substitute $\mu$ and $\sigma_\alpha$)}\\
&= 120 \pm 19.6
&& \text{(multiply)}\\
&= [100.4, 139.6]
&& \text{(add and subtract)}
\end{aligned}
$$

The quantity this model is built to estimate is $\sigma_\alpha$,
which describes all patients in the population,
not only the 20 patients who happen to be in the study.
:::
